study.title: Matthew 5 The Sermon on the Mount and the Kingdom Justice
study.overview: Matthew 5 presents the beginning of the great sermon of Jesus, a practical teaching that defines the righteousness of the Kingdom of God. The chapter begins with the Beatitudes, describing the kind of person who is truly happy before God, and follows with the image of the disciples as salt of the earth and light of the world. Then Jesus states that he did not come to abolish the Law and the Prophets, but to lead them to its fulfillment, and then deepens several commandments, showing that the righteousness of the Kingdom reaches not only external acts, but also intentions, words, relationships and desires of the heart. The climax of the chapter calls the disciples to perfection, understood as maturity, completeness and consecration to God, with love in the center.

outline.title: The Beatitudes and the Joy of the Persecuted
outline.explanation: Jesus inaugurates the sermon by happy declaring the humble, those who weep, the meek, the hungry for righteousness, the merciful, the cleans of heart, the peacemakers and those persecuted for righteousness. The promised happiness does not depend on circumstances, but on the relationship with God and the hope of the Kingdom, culminating in the call to joy even under opposition because of Christ.

outline.title: Salt and light; the justice greater than that of the religious
outline.explanation: The disciples must influence the world to the glory of God, as salt that preserves and gives taste and as visible light that illuminates the house. Jesus then declares that he came to fulfill the Law and the Prophets and demands a justice superior to that of the scribes and Pharisees, showing that the obedience of the Kingdom is not superficial, but concrete and deeper than mere religious appearance.

outline.title: The heart behind murder, adultery and divorce
outline.explanation: Jesus does not annul the commandments, but reveals his inner reach: unjust wrath is already blameable, reconciliation has priority over offering, unclean desire already contaminates the heart, and sin must be treated with radicality. Divorce is also placed under serious moral responsibility, strengthening the sanctity of bonds and the seriousness of the purity of the heart.

outline.title: Truth, meekness, generosity and love of enemies
outline.explanation: Jesus corrects the light use of the oaths and calls his disciples to an intact, simple and reliable speech. Afterwards, he replaces the logic of revenge with answers of meekness, generosity, and willingness to suffer injustice without retribution. Finally, he orders to love enemies and concludes with the requirement to be perfect as the Father, that is, matured, complete and marked by love.

study.context: The text is presented as a great discourse of Jesus on the mount, addressed to the disciples in the presence of the crowds. The notes provided highlight that this is the first of five long discourses of Matthew and that his unifying theme is the call of the Messiah to justice. It is also relevant that the way of teaching Jesus follows the custom of sitting to instruct, which indicates solemn and authoritative teaching.
study.theology: Matthew 5 teaches that the righteousness of the Kingdom is not mere external conformism, but integral obedience to the will of God revealed by Jesus. The Beatitudes show that the pattern of the Kingdom values dependence on God, purity, mercy, peace, and perseverance under persecution. The metaphor of salt and light indicates that the life of the disciples must produce very real in the world and glorify the Father. By stating that he came to fulfill the Law and the Prophets, Jesus shows continuity with the Scriptures, but also authority to interpret them in depth. The antitheses of the chapter reveal that sin begins in the heart: anger, greed, falsehood and vengeance are treated as serious even before they become visible actions. The final call to perfection must be read, according to the notes, such as maturity, wholeness and total consecration to God, having love as a core.

scholarViews.insight: The sermon on the mount has as a unifying theme the Messiah's call to justice; here justice is to do the will of God as Jesus reveals it, and this unites the whole discourse.
Jesus begins the sermon with blessings, showing that he came not only to buy blessings, but to pronounce them on his own; his statement makes those whom he blesses happy.
The order not to resist evil and to act meekly in the offenses shows a posture of no violent retribution and willingness to suffer injustice without vengeful spirit.

questions: In which areas my religious life is only external, and in which does it reflect the deepest justice that Jesus requires?
Does my way of speaking, reacting and dealing with conflicts reveals integrity and love, or just defense of myself?
How can I be salt and light in a concrete way this week, serving and glorifying God without seeking religious appearance?
study.practice: Choose a concrete attitude to practice the justice of the Kingdom this week: to be reconciled to someone, to abandon a double or offensive speech, or to respond meekly to a provocation. Also review your heart before God, asking him to purify intentions, desires and motivations, and not just visible behaviors. Try to do a good work in secret or without self-promotion, so that glory will go to the Father and not to you.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are selective and do not cover each verse; therefore, some applications and connections were made directly from the biblical text of the chapter, without explicit support for verse by verse commentary. There are also no broad historical details about the original audience in addition to being one of Jesus' speeches in Matthew and the scene occurring on the hill. The term translated as 'perfects' is interpreted in the notes as maturity, wholeness and consecration, and not as absolute impeccability.
